title: Joining the union and the black local 496's books
summary: Ridgley's in-and-out union membership since 1949, bought cards, double books at the black local.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well I want to ask you this because we were going to, I don't know if we have enough tape. Okay.
No I'm talking just in general.
There is enough tape for this question. I wanted to talk about the union. And uh. That's true.
So, when did you join the union?

Well I've been, I've been in and out the union since 1949. Like the way you said that in and out. Yeah. Well I was, I, you know I would be in and then I would drop out and then I would get back in and drop out. Well I've been in this stretch, this stretch I've been in since 19, I think since 1960. Oh, oh maybe before that. I don't think I dropped out. I think I transferred over from when they integrated it too. So maybe I've been in now, this time. No I just straightened up. So it got to be in the late 60s, maybe about 67, maybe before then. I've been in since then. But before that I was in and out. See because when we had the black local, you know, first of all they said I owed them a whole lot of tax, but I paid them. But they also had two set of books. There was the secretary who, you know, you were going there and paying, she'd mark it up in this book and then put it in that book. Well they never did prosecute nobody, but a lot of money went another way. It was the black, 496. You see, I know personally I had bought union cards. See like if I had to go to like Pritchett, Alabama, because we would all go that way. If I go to Florida, you had to have a union card. I'd go there and get a lady ten dollars and get me a union card, pay it up. But I just had to remember that Monday morning I had to come back to the hall and tear it up in front of her.
So the unions were pretty strict, wherever you played, they would check?
